summary.text: A 65-year-old man presented to the outpatient clinic with left inguinal pain during daily activities. His history included hypertension and hypercholesterolemia managed with amlodipine and atorvastatin, no prior urological history, and a cholecystectomy 3 years earlier. Examination showed a reducible left indirect inguinal hernia without scrotal involvement.

He underwent laparoscopic TAPP for the left inguinal hernia without immediate complications. Postoperatively he developed a painful inguinal hematoma, which was managed conservatively, with gradual resolution of the hematoma and the associated pain.

Eight months after surgery he returned with persistent left scrotal pain, increased scrotal size, moderate pain (VAS 4) and episodes of intense pain (VAS 9) on palpation, with swelling and tenderness of the left testicle. Ultrasound showed a fluid collection of about 4 x 1.5 cm around the left testicle, with normal echogenicity and blood flow in both testicles.

He was referred to urology; by the consultation 1 month later his pain had subsided, occurring only upon direct contact with the testicle, and the urologist concluded that surgical intervention was not indicated. The abstract describes conservative management with symptoms gradually resolving without surgery.

summary.text: A 70-year-old man presented with right-sided inguinal pain increasingly affecting his daily activities. He had managed a right inguinal hernia with a hernia belt for 1.5 years and had ischemic heart disease and hypercholesterolemia treated with bisoprolol, aspirin and rosuvastatin, plus a 2015 CABG after a myocardial infarction. Examination found a reducible right indirect inguinoscrotal hernia.

He underwent laparoscopic TAPP. Findings were a large fibrotic hernia sac with dense adhesions containing small intestine and cecum; initial mobilization failed because of fibrosis, the surgeons opted to incise the sac, a Progrip mesh was placed and the peritoneum closed with sutures.

Two weeks postoperatively he had right inguinal and scrotal pain, swelling, tenderness and induration. CT showed a 78 x 43 x 45 mm isodense lesion consistent with a hematoma, expectant management was chosen with follow-up in 2 months, and by that visit the swelling had largely subsided with no pain.

Four months postoperatively he returned with progressive scrotal swelling and pain and pronounced swelling and tenderness of the right testicle. Ultrasound showed a fluid collection of about 3 x 1 cm with normal echogenicity and blood flow in both testicles. One month later pain had resolved with mild tenderness; urology judged surgery unnecessary. The abstract notes persistent scrotal swelling and tenderness prompting further evaluation.

source_coverage.note: Abstract: names the first and second patient with age, sex, laterality and timing; used for hydrocele, hematoma and management facts.

States both adult patients developed reactive scrotal hydroceles after laparoscopic TAPP hernioplasty; used for approach and hydrocele diagnosis.
Discussion of incidence and specialty separation; no patient-specific facts.
Describes a published 2023 case report of a 59-year-old; not an index patient.
Hypothesized mechanism and conclusions; speculative and not recorded as patient facts.

article_limitations: No figures or supplements are listed in the source.
The discussion hypothesizes that postoperative hematomas evolved into hydroceles by compressing lymphatic vessels; this is speculation and is not recorded as a patient fact.
The 59-year-old patient in the discussion belongs to a cited 2023 case report and is not an index patient.
The two TAPP operations were performed within a 5-week interval at the same facility; the interval is between the two patients and is not assigned to either one.
Patient 1 hydrocele is named only in the abstract and the introduction sentence; the case narrative describes the left scrotal fluid collection on ultrasound without the word hydrocele.

Abstract says symptoms gradually resolved without surgery, while the case text keeps pain on direct contact (patient 1) and mild tenderness on palpation (patient 2); both are recorded as written, not reconciled.
Patient 2 is said to have no significant surgical history despite a documented 2015 CABG; the absent surgical-history item is kept review_only (ambiguous qualifier).
